questions.question: What is the size of float and double in Java?
questions.subject: Java Basics – Features, JVM, Data Types, Operators, Control Statements and Arrays

options.A: Byte code is executed by JVM
options.B: The applet makes the Java code secure & portable

questions.subject: Java Basics – Features, JVM, Data Types, Operators, Control Statements and Arrays
questions.explanation: The same bytecode runs on any JVM, which also verifies it before execution. (Official answer: KEA final key, GTTC recruitment 2024.)

questions.question: Which component is used to compile, debug and execute the Java Programs?
questions.subject: Java Basics – Features, JVM, Data Types, Operators, Control Statements and Arrays
questions.explanation: JDK = JRE + development tools (javac, jdb, javadoc…); JRE = JVM + libraries. (Official answer: KEA final key, GTTC recruitment 2024.)

questions.question: Which of the following operators is used to allocate memory to array variable in Java?
questions.subject: Java Basics – Features, JVM, Data Types, Operators, Control Statements and Arrays
questions.explanation: int[] a = new int[5]; Java has no malloc. (Answer worked out by ExamSim; not KEA's official key.)

questions.question: Java was developed by ____ at Sun Microsystems and released in 1995 (it was first called Oak).
questions.subject: Java Basics – Features, JVM, Data Types, Operators, Control Statements and Arrays
questions.explanation: PYQ pattern (KEA / KSET papers). Stroustrup – C++; Ritchie – C; van Rossum – Python.

questions.question: The Java compiler (javac) converts source code into:
questions.subject: Java Basics – Features, JVM, Data Types, Operators, Control Statements and Arrays
questions.explanation: The JVM interprets bytecode or compiles hot parts to native code with the JIT compiler.

questions.question: The JIT (Just-In-Time) compiler in the JVM:

options.B: Compiles frequently executed bytecode to native machine code at run time to improve speed

questions.subject: Java Basics – Features, JVM, Data Types, Operators, Control Statements and Arrays
questions.explanation: PYQ pattern (KEA / KSET papers). Garbage collection removes unused objects.

questions.question: How many primitive data types does Java have?

options.C: 8 – byte, short, int, long, float, double, char, boolean

questions.subject: Java Basics – Features, JVM, Data Types, Operators, Control Statements and Arrays
questions.explanation: String is a class, not a primitive type.

questions.question: The size of char in Java is:
questions.subject: Java Basics – Features, JVM, Data Types, Operators, Control Statements and Arrays
questions.explanation: PYQ pattern (KEA / KSET papers). Java uses UTF-16 code units for char.

questions.question: The range of the byte data type in Java is:
questions.subject: Java Basics – Features, JVM, Data Types, Operators, Control Statements and Arrays
questions.explanation: byte – 8 bits; short – 16; int – 32; long – 64.

questions.subject: Java Basics – Features, JVM, Data Types, Operators, Control Statements and Arrays
questions.explanation: PYQ pattern (KEA / KSET papers). x++ gives 10 (x becomes 11), ++x makes x 12 and gives 12 → 10 + 12 = 22.

questions.question:
What is printed?
System.out.println(5 / 2 + 5 % 2);
questions.subject: Java Basics – Features, JVM, Data Types, Operators, Control Statements and Arrays
questions.explanation: Integer division 5/2 = 2; 5 % 2 = 1; 2 + 1 = 3.

questions.question:
What is printed?
System.out.println(1 + 2 + "A" + 1 + 2);
questions.subject: Java Basics – Features, JVM, Data Types, Operators, Control Statements and Arrays
questions.explanation: PYQ pattern (KEA / KSET papers). Left to right: 1 + 2 = 3, then string concatenation: "3A" + 1 + 2 = "3A12".

options.A: Compile-time error: possible lossy conversion from int to byte

questions.subject: Java Basics – Features, JVM, Data Types, Operators, Control Statements and Arrays
questions.explanation: b + 1 is promoted to int; an explicit cast (byte)(b + 1) or b += 1 is needed.

questions.question: The value of (int) 3.99 in Java is:
questions.subject: Java Basics – Features, JVM, Data Types, Operators, Control Statements and Arrays
questions.explanation: PYQ pattern (KEA / KSET papers). Narrowing a floating value to int truncates toward zero.

questions.question: Which Java operator is the unsigned right shift?
questions.subject: Java Basics – Features, JVM, Data Types, Operators, Control Statements and Arrays
questions.explanation: >> keeps the sign bit; >>> fills with zeros.

questions.question: Since which version can a switch statement in Java use String values?
questions.subject: Java Basics – Features, JVM, Data Types, Operators, Control Statements and Arrays
questions.explanation: PYQ pattern (KEA / KSET papers). Switch also works with byte, short, char, int, their wrappers and enums.

questions.subject: Java Basics – Features, JVM, Data Types, Operators, Control Statements and Arrays
questions.explanation: Array elements default to 0; a.length is a field (3), not a method.

questions.question: Accessing a[5] in an array of length 5 throws:
questions.subject: Java Basics – Features, JVM, Data Types, Operators, Control Statements and Arrays
questions.explanation: PYQ pattern (KEA / KSET papers). Indices run from 0 to length − 1.

questions.question: A 'jagged' array in Java is:

options.D: A two-dimensional array whose rows have different lengths

questions.subject: Java Basics – Features, JVM, Data Types, Operators, Control Statements and Arrays
questions.explanation: int[][] t = new int[3][]; t[0] = new int[2]; t[1] = new int[5]; …

questions.question: The correct signature of the main method used by the JVM is:
questions.subject: Java Basics – Features, JVM, Data Types, Operators, Control Statements and Arrays
questions.explanation: PYQ pattern (KEA / KSET papers). It must be public (callable by JVM) and static (called without an object).

questions.question: Which of these words is reserved in Java but NOT used?
questions.subject: Java Basics – Features, JVM, Data Types, Operators, Control Statements and Arrays
questions.explanation: goto and const are reserved keywords with no meaning in Java.

questions.question:
What is printed?
for (int i = 0; i < 5; i++) { if (i == 3) break; System.out.print(i); }
questions.subject: Java Basics – Features, JVM, Data Types, Operators, Control Statements and Arrays
questions.explanation: PYQ pattern (KEA / KSET papers). The loop stops when i becomes 3.

questions.subject: Java Basics – Features, JVM, Data Types, Operators, Control Statements and Arrays
questions.explanation: The ternary operator ?: chooses one of two values.

questions.question: The enhanced for loop 'for (int v : arr)' is used to:

options.A: Iterate over every element of an array or collection without an index

questions.subject: Java Basics – Features, JVM, Data Types, Operators, Control Statements and Arrays
questions.explanation: PYQ pattern (KEA / KSET papers). It was introduced in Java 5.

questions.question: Local variables in Java:

options.B: Are initialised by the garbage collector
options.C: Must be initialised before use; they get no default value

questions.subject: Java Basics – Features, JVM, Data Types, Operators, Control Statements and Arrays
questions.explanation: Instance and static fields do get defaults (0, false, null).

questions.question:
Assertion (A): Java is platform independent.
Reason (R): The Java compiler produces bytecode that can run on any machine with a JVM.

options.A: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
options.B: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
options.C: A is true, but R is false
options.D: A is false, but R is true

questions.subject: Java Basics – Features, JVM, Data Types, Operators, Control Statements and Arrays
questions.explanation: PYQ pattern (KEA / KSET papers). 'Write once, run anywhere'.

questions.question:
Consider the statements:
I. Java supports explicit pointers and pointer arithmetic.
II. Java has automatic garbage collection.

questions.question:
What is printed?
System.out.println(10 == 10.0);

questions.subject: Classes, Objects, Constructors, Inheritance, Interfaces and Packages

notes.title: Basic Java – revision sheet with output tracing
notes.md:
## Java facts
- **James Gosling**, Sun Microsystems, 1995 (first called **Oak**); owned by **Oracle** since 2010
- "Write once, run anywhere": `javac Hello.java` → **bytecode** `Hello.class` → `java Hello` runs it on the **JVM** (interpreter + **JIT** compiler)
- **JDK** (tools: javac, java, javadoc, jar, jdb) ⊃ **JRE** (libraries + JVM) ⊃ **JVM**
- Features: simple, **object-oriented**, platform-independent, secure (no pointers, bytecode verifier, sandbox), robust (strong typing, exceptions, **garbage collection**), multithreaded, distributed, portable
- No pointers, no multiple inheritance of classes, no operator overloading, no global variables, no `goto` (reserved word)

## Program structure
```java
public class Hello {                          // file must be Hello.java
    public static void main(String[] args) {  // entry point
        System.out.println("Hello, KRIES");
    }
}
```

## Data types (sizes are fixed on every platform)
| Type | Size | Default (fields) |
|---|---|---|
| byte | 1 byte (−128 … 127) | 0 |
| short | 2 | 0 |
| int | 4 | 0 |
| long | 8 (`10L`) | 0L |
| float | 4 (`2.5f`) | 0.0f |
| double | 8 | 0.0 |
| **char** | **2 (Unicode)** | '\u0000' |
| boolean | true/false (not 0/1) | false |
- Reference types default to **null**; **local variables have no default** – using one uninitialised is a compile error
- Widening is automatic (int → long → float → double); narrowing needs a cast: `(byte) 130` = **−126**

## Output tracing
| Code | Output | Why |
|---|---|---|
| `System.out.println(10 / 3 + " " + 10 % 3);` | 3 1 | integer division |
| `System.out.println(-10 % 3);` | -1 | sign of the left operand |
| `System.out.println(1 + 2 + "3");` | 33 | 1 + 2 = 3, then "3" + "3" |
| `System.out.println("1" + 2 + 3);` | 123 | string concatenation from the left |
| `System.out.println('A' + 1);` | 66 | char promoted to int |
| `System.out.println("" + 'A' + 1);` | A1 | |
| `char c = 'A'; c += 1; System.out.println(c);` | B | compound assignment casts back (`c = c + 1` is a compile error) |
| `int i = 5; int j = i++ + ++i;` | j = **12**, i = 7 | defined in Java: 5 + 7 (in C it is undefined) |
| `System.out.println(5.0 / 0);` | Infinity | `5 / 0` throws ArithmeticException |
| `System.out.println(Math.round(2.5) + " " + Math.round(-2.5));` | 3 -2 | floor(x + 0.5) |
| `String a = "hi", b = "hi"; a == b` | true | string pool (same literal) |
| `new String("hi") == "hi"` | false | different objects – use `.equals()` |
| `Integer x = 127, y = 127; x == y` | true | cached −128 … 127 (128 → false) |

## Classes and objects
- Access: **private** (class only) < **default** (package) < **protected** (package + subclasses) < **public**
- Constructor: same name, no return type; default constructor added only if none written; `this(...)` / `super(...)` must be the **first** statement
- `static` members belong to the class; a **static block** runs once when the class loads (before main); static methods can't use `this`
- `final` variable = constant; final method can't be overridden; final class can't be extended (String)
```java
class A { A() { System.out.print("A"); } }
class B extends A { B() { System.out.print("B"); } }
new B();                                   // AB  – superclass constructor first
class T { static int c = 0; T() { c++; } }
new T(); new T(); System.out.print(T.c);   // 2
```
- **Inheritance**: `class B extends A` (single only); **interfaces**: `class C implements I1, I2` (multiple); `abstract` classes can't be instantiated
- **Overriding** + dynamic dispatch: `A obj = new B(); obj.show();` calls B's show (methods are polymorphic, **fields are not**)
- Overloading = same name, different parameters (compile time)
- Packages: `java.lang` (imported automatically – String, Math, System, Thread), java.util (Scanner, ArrayList, HashMap), java.io, java.awt, javax.swing, java.sql, java.net

## Arrays and strings
- `int[] a = new int[5];` → all 0; `a.length` (field) vs `s.length()` (method); index out of range → ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException
- String is **immutable**; **StringBuilder** (fast, not thread-safe) and **StringBuffer** (synchronized) are mutable
- Methods: length, charAt, substring(1, 3) (end excluded), indexOf, equals, equalsIgnoreCase, compareTo, toUpperCase, trim, split, replace, concat
- `"KRIES".substring(1, 3)` → "RI"; `"abc".compareTo("abd")` → −1

## Exceptions
- `Throwable` → **Error** (OutOfMemoryError – don't catch) and **Exception** → checked (IOException, SQLException, ClassNotFoundException – must be caught or declared with `throws`) and **unchecked** RuntimeException (ArithmeticException, NullPointerException, ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException, NumberFormatException)
- `try` / `catch` (specific before general) / `finally` (always runs, except System.exit); `throw` an object, `throws` in a method header; custom exceptions extend Exception
```java
static int f() { try { return 1; } finally { System.out.print("F"); } }
System.out.print(f());                    // F1
```

## Multithreading
- Create: **extend Thread** or **implement Runnable** (preferred – the class can still extend another); call **start()** (calling run() directly runs in the same thread)
- States: new → runnable → running → blocked/waiting/timed-waiting → terminated
- `sleep(ms)`, `join()`, `yield()`, priorities 1–10 (NORM 5); `synchronized` methods/blocks for mutual exclusion; `wait()`, `notify()`, `notifyAll()` are methods of **Object**; deadlock possible

## Applets and JDBC
- Applet life cycle: **init() → start() → paint(Graphics g) → stop() → destroy()**; ran in browsers/appletviewer; no main(); **deprecated** (removed in modern JDKs) – still asked in exams
- **JDBC** steps: load driver (`Class.forName(...)`) → `DriverManager.getConnection(url, user, pwd)` → `createStatement()` / `prepareStatement()` → `executeQuery()` (SELECT → **ResultSet**) or `executeUpdate()` (INSERT/UPDATE/DELETE → row count) → close
- Driver types: **1** JDBC-ODBC bridge, **2** native-API, **3** network protocol (middleware), **4** thin / pure Java (most used)

## Traps
- `main` must be `public static void main(String[] args)`
- `==` compares references for objects; `.equals()` compares contents
- Java has `>>>` (unsigned right shift) – C does not
- `char` is 2 bytes in Java (1 in C)

questions.question: In the Digital Differential Analyser algorithm, the decision increment either x or y is based on:

options.B: The product of x and y coordinates

questions.subject: Display Devices, Line, Circle and Curve Drawing, and Filling
questions.explanation: If |m| ≤ 1 x is stepped by 1 and y by m; otherwise y is stepped by 1 and x by 1/m. (Answer worked out by ExamSim; not KEA's official key.)

questions.question: The algorithm that is typically used to compute points on a Bezier curve is
questions.subject: Display Devices, Line, Circle and Curve Drawing, and Filling
questions.explanation: de Casteljau's algorithm uses repeated linear interpolation of control points. (Answer worked out by ExamSim; not KEA's official key.)

questions.question: In a raster-scan CRT, the picture is:

options.B: Stored as intensity values in a frame (refresh) buffer and painted line by line
options.C: Drawn as lines directly by the beam from a display list

questions.subject: Display Devices, Line, Circle and Curve Drawing, and Filling
questions.explanation: PYQ pattern (KEA / KSET papers). Random-scan (vector) displays draw lines from a display file.

questions.question: A frame buffer for a 1024 × 768 display with 24 bits per pixel needs about:
questions.subject: Display Devices, Line, Circle and Curve Drawing, and Filling

questions.question: With 8 bits per pixel, the number of different colours that can be shown at once is:
questions.subject: Display Devices, Line, Circle and Curve Drawing, and Filling
questions.explanation: PYQ pattern (KEA / KSET papers). 2⁸ = 256; 24-bit 'true colour' gives about 16.7 million.

questions.question: Persistence of a phosphor is defined as:

options.C: The time for the emitted light to decay to one-tenth of its original intensity

questions.subject: Display Devices, Line, Circle and Curve Drawing, and Filling
questions.explanation: Lower persistence needs a higher refresh rate to avoid flicker.

questions.question: Aspect ratio of a display is the ratio of:

options.D: Vertical points to horizontal points needed to produce equal-length lines in both directions

questions.subject: Display Devices, Line, Circle and Curve Drawing, and Filling
questions.explanation: PYQ pattern (KEA / KSET papers). Hearn & Baker's definition; an aspect ratio of 3/4 means a vertical line plotted with 3 points equals a horizontal line with 4.

questions.question: In colour CRTs, the shadow-mask method:

options.B: Uses three electron guns and red, green and blue phosphor dot triads
options.C: Uses two phosphor layers and beam penetration

questions.subject: Display Devices, Line, Circle and Curve Drawing, and Filling
questions.explanation: Beam penetration gives only a few colours (red, orange, yellow, green).

questions.question: A direct-view storage tube (DVST):

options.B: Keeps the picture without refreshing but cannot selectively erase parts

questions.subject: Display Devices, Line, Circle and Curve Drawing, and Filling
questions.explanation: PYQ pattern (KEA / KSET papers). The picture is stored as a charge distribution behind the phosphor; erasing needs the whole screen to be cleared.

questions.question: Interlaced refresh means:

options.A: Odd scan lines are drawn in one pass and even lines in the next
options.C: Only half the screen is ever drawn

questions.subject: Display Devices, Line, Circle and Curve Drawing, and Filling
questions.explanation: It reduces flicker on low refresh rates.

questions.question: DDA from (2, 3) to (6, 5): the number of steps and the increments (Δx, Δy) per step are:
questions.subject: Display Devices, Line, Circle and Curve Drawing, and Filling
questions.explanation: PYQ pattern (KEA / KSET papers). dx = 4, dy = 2, steps = max(|dx|, |dy|) = 4; increments dx/4 and dy/4.

questions.question: The main disadvantage of DDA compared with Bresenham's algorithm is that DDA:

options.C: Uses floating-point arithmetic and rounding, which is slower and accumulates error

questions.subject: Display Devices, Line, Circle and Curve Drawing, and Filling
questions.explanation: Rounding of floating-point values at every step also makes long lines drift from the true path.

questions.question: For Bresenham's line from (20, 10) to (30, 18), the initial decision parameter p0 = 2Δy − Δx is:
questions.subject: Display Devices, Line, Circle and Curve Drawing, and Filling
questions.explanation: PYQ pattern (KEA / KSET papers). Δx = 10, Δy = 8 → p0 = 16 − 10 = 6.

questions.question: For the same line, p0 = 6 ≥ 0, so the next pixel is (21, 11). The next decision parameter p1 is:
questions.subject: Display Devices, Line, Circle and Curve Drawing, and Filling
questions.explanation: p ≥ 0 → y increments and p1 = p0 + 2Δy − 2Δx = 6 + 16 − 20 = 2.

questions.question: For the midpoint circle algorithm with radius r = 10, the initial decision parameter p0 = 1 − r is:
questions.subject: Display Devices, Line, Circle and Curve Drawing, and Filling
questions.explanation: PYQ pattern (KEA / KSET papers). Pixels are generated in one octant and mirrored using eight-way symmetry.

questions.question: In Bresenham's circle algorithm, the initial decision variable is d = 3 − 2r. For r = 10 it is:
questions.subject: Display Devices, Line, Circle and Curve Drawing, and Filling

questions.question: A circle-drawing algorithm needs to compute points in only one octant because of:
questions.subject: Display Devices, Line, Circle and Curve Drawing, and Filling
questions.explanation: PYQ pattern (KEA / KSET papers). An ellipse has four-way symmetry.

questions.question: The midpoint ellipse algorithm divides the first quadrant into two regions according to:

options.C: Where the slope of the curve becomes −1

questions.subject: Display Devices, Line, Circle and Curve Drawing, and Filling
questions.explanation: In region 1 (|slope| < 1) x is stepped; in region 2 (|slope| > 1) y is stepped.

questions.question: The boundary-fill and flood-fill algorithms can use:
questions.subject: Display Devices, Line, Circle and Curve Drawing, and Filling
questions.explanation: PYQ pattern (KEA / KSET papers). Scan-line polygon filling uses edge intersections and an active edge list.

questions.question: The odd–even (even–odd) rule decides whether a point is inside a polygon by:

options.B: Counting edge crossings of a ray from the point: odd = inside

questions.subject: Display Devices, Line, Circle and Curve Drawing, and Filling
questions.explanation: The nonzero winding-number rule is the other inside–outside test.

questions.question: The 'staircase' or jagged appearance of lines on raster displays is called aliasing; it is reduced by:

options.D: Antialiasing techniques such as supersampling and area sampling

questions.subject: Display Devices, Line, Circle and Curve Drawing, and Filling
questions.explanation: PYQ pattern (KEA / KSET papers). Aliasing comes from sampling a continuous line at discrete pixels; antialiasing varies pixel intensities along the edge.

questions.question: A Bezier curve with 4 control points is of degree:
questions.subject: Display Devices, Line, Circle and Curve Drawing, and Filling
questions.explanation: Degree = number of control points − 1; it passes through the first and last points and lies in the convex hull.

questions.question: Compared with Bezier curves, B-splines offer:

options.B: Local control – moving one control point affects only part of the curve

questions.subject: Display Devices, Line, Circle and Curve Drawing, and Filling
questions.explanation: PYQ pattern (KEA / KSET papers). The degree of a B-spline is independent of the number of control points; Bezier curves have global control.

questions.question: Which is a graphics standard/API?
questions.subject: Display Devices, Line, Circle and Curve Drawing, and Filling
questions.explanation: GKS and PHIGS are older graphics standards.

questions.question: A light pen is used to:

options.D: Select screen positions by detecting light from the CRT

questions.subject: Display Devices, Line, Circle and Curve Drawing, and Filling
questions.explanation: PYQ pattern (KEA / KSET papers). Other input devices: tablet (digitiser), joystick, mouse, touch panel.

questions.question:
Assertion (A): Bresenham's line algorithm is faster than DDA.
Reason (R): It uses only integer addition, subtraction and multiplication by 2.

options.A: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
options.B: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
options.C: A is true, but R is false
options.D: A is false, but R is true

questions.subject: Display Devices, Line, Circle and Curve Drawing, and Filling
questions.explanation: No floating-point operations or rounding are needed.

questions.question:
Consider the statements:
I. A random-scan display draws pictures as a set of line segments.
II. A raster-scan display stores the picture as an array of pixel intensities in a frame buffer.
questions.subject: Display Devices, Line, Circle and Curve Drawing, and Filling
questions.explanation: PYQ pattern (KEA / KSET papers). Both are correct.

questions.question: In a raster scan, the return of the beam to the left of the next line is called:
questions.subject: Display Devices, Line, Circle and Curve Drawing, and Filling
questions.explanation: At the end of each frame the beam returns to the top left – vertical retrace.

questions.question: LCD (liquid crystal display) screens produce images by:

options.C: Passing polarised light through liquid crystals that twist or align to block or pass light

questions.subject: Display Devices, Line, Circle and Curve Drawing, and Filling
questions.explanation: PYQ pattern (KEA / KSET papers). Plasma panels use ionised gas; LED displays use light-emitting diodes.

questions.question: Resolution of a display is:

options.D: The maximum number of points (pixels) that can be displayed without overlap

questions.subject: Display Devices, Line, Circle and Curve Drawing, and Filling
questions.explanation: It is usually stated as pixels across × down, e.g. 1920 × 1080.

questions.subject: 2-D Transformations, Windowing, Clipping, Colour Models and Projections

questions.question: In the Cohen-Sutherland line clipping algorithm, the region codes (out codes) are:

questions.question: Homogeneous coordinates are used in 2-D graphics so that:

options.B: Translation, rotation and scaling can all be represented as 3 × 3 matrix multiplications and composed

questions.subject: 2-D Transformations, Windowing, Clipping, Colour Models and Projections
questions.explanation: PYQ pattern (KEA / KSET papers). A 2-D point (x, y) becomes (x, y, 1).

questions.subject: 2-D Transformations, Windowing, Clipping, Colour Models and Projections

questions.question: Rotating the point (3, 4) by 90° anticlockwise about the origin gives:
questions.subject: 2-D Transformations, Windowing, Clipping, Colour Models and Projections
questions.explanation: PYQ pattern (KEA / KSET papers). x' = x cos θ − y sin θ, y' = x sin θ + y cos θ; for 90°: (−y, x).

questions.explanation: PYQ pattern (KEA / KSET papers). x' = x + shx·y = 2 + 6 = 8; y unchanged.

questions.question: Two successive translations (tx1, ty1) and (tx2, ty2) are equivalent to:

options.B: A single translation (tx1 + tx2, ty1 + ty2)

questions.subject: 2-D Transformations, Windowing, Clipping, Colour Models and Projections
questions.explanation: PYQ pattern (KEA / KSET papers). Two rotations add angles; two scalings multiply factors.

questions.question: Which transformations are 'rigid-body' (preserve lengths and angles)?
questions.subject: 2-D Transformations, Windowing, Clipping, Colour Models and Projections
questions.explanation: Uniform scaling preserves shape (angles) but not size.

questions.question: In computer graphics, a 'window' and a 'viewport' are respectively:

options.A: A device area and a world area
options.B: The area of the world-coordinate scene selected for display, and the area on the display device where it is shown
options.D: A colour table and a frame buffer

questions.subject: 2-D Transformations, Windowing, Clipping, Colour Models and Projections
questions.explanation: PYQ pattern (KEA / KSET papers). Window = what to show; viewport = where to show it.

questions.question: Window (0,0)–(10,10) is mapped to viewport (0,0)–(100,50). The point (5,5) maps to:
questions.subject: 2-D Transformations, Windowing, Clipping, Colour Models and Projections

questions.subject: 2-D Transformations, Windowing, Clipping, Colour Models and Projections
questions.explanation: PYQ pattern (KEA / KSET papers). Panning moves a fixed-size window across the scene.

questions.question: In Cohen–Sutherland clipping, a line is trivially ACCEPTED when:

options.B: The logical AND of the codes is non-zero

questions.subject: 2-D Transformations, Windowing, Clipping, Colour Models and Projections
questions.explanation: It is trivially rejected when the logical AND of the two codes is non-zero (both ends on the same outside side).

questions.question: For window xmin = 0, xmax = 10, ymin = 0, ymax = 10 and bit order TBRL (top, bottom, right, left), the region code of point (12, 5) is:
questions.subject: 2-D Transformations, Windowing, Clipping, Colour Models and Projections
questions.explanation: PYQ pattern (KEA / KSET papers). x > xmax sets the 'right' bit only.

questions.explanation: Cyrus–Beck is the general parametric method for convex windows.

questions.question: The Sutherland–Hodgman algorithm is used for:

options.C: Polygon clipping against each window edge in turn

questions.question: A point (x, y) is retained by point clipping if:

questions.question: The RGB colour model is ____ and is used in ____.
questions.subject: 2-D Transformations, Windowing, Clipping, Colour Models and Projections
questions.explanation: PYQ pattern (KEA / KSET papers). Red + green + blue at full intensity give white.

options.D: Compares depth values per pixel and keeps the nearest surface

questions.question: Back-face detection removes polygons whose:

questions.explanation: The scaling matrix has sx and sy on the diagonal.

Assertion (A): Rotating and then translating an object always gives the same result as translating and then rotating it.
Reason (R): Matrix multiplication is, in general, not commutative.

options.A: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
options.B: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A

options.D: A is false, but R is true

questions.question:
Consider the statements about Cohen–Sutherland clipping:
I. A line with both end-point codes 0000 is trivially accepted.
II. If the logical AND of the two codes is non-zero, the line must be subdivided and clipped further.

questions.question: Uniform scaling means:

options.C: sx = sy, so the shape is preserved

questions.subject: 2-D Transformations, Windowing, Clipping, Colour Models and Projections
questions.explanation: PYQ pattern (KEA / KSET papers). Negative factors also reflect the object.

options.B: Repeatedly divides a partially visible line at its mid-point until the visible part is found

questions.subject: 2-D Transformations, Windowing, Clipping, Colour Models and Projections
questions.explanation: It suits hardware implementation because dividing by 2 is a shift operation.

notes.title: Computer graphics – revision sheet with worked algorithms
notes.md:
## Display devices
- **CRT**: electron gun → deflection → phosphor screen; persistence; refresh rate (60 Hz+)
- **Raster scan**: beam sweeps every line; picture in a **frame buffer** (refresh buffer); interlaced/non-interlaced; TV, monitors; jagged lines (aliasing)
- **Random scan (vector)**: draws lines directly; smooth lines; display file; no realistic shading
- Flat panels: LCD, LED, plasma; colour CRT – **shadow mask** (RGB dots) or beam penetration
- **Resolution** = pixels (1024 × 768); **aspect ratio** = width/height (4 : 3, 16 : 9)
- **Frame buffer size** = width × height × bits per pixel / 8
  - 1024 × 768 × 24-bit = 2,359,296 bytes = **2.25 MB**; 640 × 480 × 8-bit = **307,200 bytes**; 24 bits → 2²⁴ ≈ 16.7 million colours
- Input: light pen, digitiser, joystick, touch panel; graphics software: OpenGL, DirectX

## Line drawing
**DDA** (digital differential analyser): steps = max(|Δx|, |Δy|); add Δx/steps and Δy/steps each step, round
- (2, 3) → (10, 8): steps 8, x += 1, y += 0.625 → (2, 3) (3, 4) (4, 4) (5, 5) (6, 6) (7, 6) (8, 7) (9, 7) (10, 8)
- Uses floating point and rounding → slower

**Bresenham** (integers only), for 0 < slope < 1: p₀ = 2Δy − Δx; if p < 0 → (x + 1, y), p += 2Δy; else → (x + 1, y + 1), p += 2Δy − 2Δx
- (20, 10) → (30, 18): Δx = 10, Δy = 8, **p₀ = 6**; pixels (21, 11) (22, 12) (23, 12) (24, 13) (25, 14) (26, 15) (27, 16) (28, 16) (29, 17) (30, 18)

## Circles, ellipses, curves
- **Midpoint circle**: start (0, r), p₀ = 1 − r; if p < 0 → (x + 1, y), p += 2x + 1; else → (x + 1, y − 1), p += 2(x − y) + 1 (with the new x, y); compute one **octant**, mirror to 8 (8-way symmetry)
  - r = 10: (0, 10) (1, 10) (2, 10) (3, 10) (4, 9) (5, 9) (6, 8) (7, 7)
- Ellipse: midpoint algorithm with 4-way symmetry, two regions
- **Bezier curve**: n + 1 control points → degree n; passes through the **first and last** points; inside the **convex hull**; global control (moving one point changes the whole curve); Bernstein polynomials
- **B-spline**: **local control**, degree independent of the number of points

## Filling
- **Scan-line** polygon fill (edge table, active edge list, fill between pairs of intersections)
- **Boundary fill** – fill until the boundary colour; **flood fill** – replace one interior colour; **4-connected** (up/down/left/right) vs **8-connected** (+ diagonals); recursive versions use a stack
- Inside test: odd–even (crossing) rule, non-zero winding rule

## 2-D transformations (homogeneous coordinates, 3 × 3 matrices)
| Transform | Result for (x, y) |
|---|---|
| Translation (tx, ty) | (x + tx, y + ty) |
| Scaling (sx, sy) about origin | (sx·x, sy·y) → (2, 3) with sx = 2, sy = 0.5 → (4, 1.5) |
| Rotation θ (anticlockwise) about origin | (x cos θ − y sin θ, x sin θ + y cos θ) → (4, 3) by 90° → **(−3, 4)** |
| Reflection about x-axis / y-axis / origin / y = x | (x, −y) / (−x, y) / (−x, −y) / (y, x) |
| Shear in x | (x + shx·y, y) |
- **Composite** transforms multiply matrices (order matters – not commutative); rotation/scaling about a fixed point (xp, yp) = T(xp, yp) · R(θ) · T(−xp, −yp)
- Homogeneous coordinates let translation be a matrix multiplication too

## Windowing and clipping
- **Window** = area of the world selected (world coordinates); **viewport** = area on the screen (device coordinates)
- Mapping: xv = xvmin + (xw − xwmin) · sx, sx = (xvmax − xvmin)/(xwmax − xwmin) (same for y)
  - Window (10, 10)–(110, 60) → viewport (0, 0)–(200, 100): sx = sy = 2 → point (60, 35) maps to **(100, 50)**
- **Cohen–Sutherland** line clipping: 4-bit **outcode TBRL** (top, bottom, right, left); window (0, 0)–(10, 10): (12, −3) → **0110**, (−2, 15) → **1001**; both codes 0000 → accept; codes AND ≠ 0 → reject; else clip
- **Liang–Barsky** (parametric, faster), Cyrus–Beck; **Sutherland–Hodgman** polygon clipping (clip against each edge in turn), Weiler–Atherton (concave polygons)

## Colour models
| Model | Type | Use |
|---|---|---|
| **RGB** | additive (light): R + G + B = white | monitors |
| **CMY(K)** | subtractive (ink): C = 1 − R … | printers |
| **HSV / HSB** | hue, saturation, value | user colour pickers |
| YIQ | luminance + chrominance | NTSC TV |

## Projections (3-D → 2-D)
- **Parallel**: projectors parallel; **orthographic** (perpendicular to the plane – front/top/side views, isometric) and **oblique** (cavalier, cabinet); preserves relative proportions
- **Perspective**: projectors meet at the centre of projection; distant objects look smaller (**foreshortening**); 1-, 2-, 3-point perspective by **vanishing points**
- 3-D: back-face removal, **z-buffer (depth buffer)** hidden-surface method, ray tracing; shading – flat, Gouraud (interpolate intensities), Phong (interpolate normals)

## Traps
- Bresenham uses only **integer** arithmetic; DDA uses floating point
- Circle has **8**-way symmetry, ellipse **4**-way
- Bezier curves pass through only the end control points
- RGB is additive, CMY subtractive
